extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, students, and journalists interested in news theory and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Carey's ritual-vs-transmission framework to evaluate or code news selection and placement decisions, emphasizing community-affirming functions alongside information utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission View — quality: accuracy, fidelity, reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication = sending information across geography for control. Quality measure: accuracy, fidelity, reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from telegraph and mass-media-as-common-carriers thinking; ideology characterized as instrumental rationality. Use this axis to judge stories by information utility and technical success of transmission (timeliness, factual correctness, breadth of distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual View — quality: confirmation, reaffirmation, communal binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication = 'the maintenance of society in time' through 'the representation of shared beliefs.' Quality measure: confirmation, reaffirmation, communal binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from religious worship and communal storytelling; ideology: meaning-making and identity-confirmation. Use this axis to judge stories by how they sustain shared worldviews and social identity rather than by pure informational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory Stories Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that confirm the shared world picture (pillars of society, predictable rhythms) are systematically preferred over stories that challenge it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection bias toward narratives that reassure and reproduce existing cultural categories; anti-patterns include privileging disruptive/challenging stories that undermine the shared order. Useful for predicting which beats get placement despite low informational novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily Rhythm Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: News must arrive on schedule and in expected form; the ritual is disrupted if the morning paper is empty or chaotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness here is about ritual timing (morning paper, evening broadcast) and format consistency. Stories that fit expected rhythms score higher on ritual newsworthiness even if they offer less new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Anniversaries, holidays, transitions of power, deaths, season-openers all have inherent news value because they ritually reaffirm communal time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These events have a 'ceremonial-event premium'—coverage exceeds information value because it performs communal reaffirmation. Coders should flag ceremonial structure as a ritual marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-Marking Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Local high-school sports, obituaries, weather are massively over-represented relative to information value because they perform community membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat topics that mark community identity as high ritual-value features. Expect disproportionate coverage of such topics in local outlets; consider them normative signals of membership rather than purely informational beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassurance Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorder stories must include closure or restoration narrative ('the situation is being addressed') to fit the reassurance function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ritual compatibility, stories about crises are packaged to show resolution or institutional response. Lack of closure undermines the reassurance role and may reduce ritual newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Self-Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about readers' own demographic/community are most newsworthy; readers want to see themselves represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors representation and demographic/community resonance. Use audience-affinity markers when coding for ritual salience (e.g., explicit community references, local names, shared identifiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper-as-Ritual Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading the newspaper performs ritual tasks: confirms a shared world picture, affirms social membership ('we are the kind of people who care about these things'), performs civic identity (informed citizenship), and reproduces cultural categories (what counts as important).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news, consider these social functions as goals distinct from information transmission. Stories that perform one or more of these functions rate higher on ritual newsworthiness; absence of these functions is an anti-pattern for ritual-oriented selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-axis Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: An event can be high or low on transmission-view newsworthiness (information utility) AND high or low on ritual-view newsworthiness (community-identity affirmation). Front-page selection often privileges the latter even when the former is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bivariate coding scheme (transmission axis × ritual axis) to predict placement and prominence. Note that high ritual / low transmission events may still get top placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability: code for ritual markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories can be coded for ritual markers (community references, identity-affirming framing, ceremonial structure) as features in placement-prediction models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of ritual markers to operationalize: explicit community identifiers (local institutions, high-school teams), anniversaries/ceremonies, narratives of restoration, obituary formats, routine timetabled features. Useful for mixed-methods or computational models predicting front-page placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction — Why local news survives
rubrics_metrics.description: Local news performs ritual identity-affirmation that national news cannot replace, explaining its persistence even in the digital era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate local outlets for ritual functions (community-marking, audience self-recognition) rather than information uniqueness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction — Why morning routines persist
rubrics_metrics.description: News-consumption rituals (morning newspaper, evening broadcast, Sunday talk shows) survive because they perform the ritual function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess routines as ritual practices; disruption to routines (e.g., irregular delivery) reduces ritual value even if information is available elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction — Why sensational outliers persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that puncture the shared world picture (mass shootings, natural disasters) require more coverage because they demand collective ritual processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These events gain coverage not merely for informational urgency but for communal meaning-making; expect intensified ritual framing and repeated narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction — Why obituaries matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Death notices perform communal acknowledgment of membership and loss — high ritual value, low information value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat obituaries as quintessential ritual content; their prominence signals community bonds and membership recognition rather than novel information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction — Why repetition is a feature, not a bug
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-narrating the same touchstone events (anniversaries, commemorations) is ritual work; from the transmission view it looks like information waste, from the ritual view it is the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or auditing coverage, count repetition of ritual events as intentional reinforcement of shared meanings rather than editorial laziness.
